influences/rhetoric-and-education/name: Classical rhetoric, education and the Christian intellectual tradition
influences/rhetoric-and-education/source: Greek paideia and Roman education: the grammarian, the rhetor, the liberal arts and the canon of classical authors
influences/rhetoric-and-education/christ: Christian preaching and exegesis shaped by rhetoric, the ‘spoiling of the Egyptians’, monastic copying of classics, the seven liberal arts, cathedral schools and universities
influences/rhetoric-and-education/eviden: Christian use of the classical school system and of rhetorical theory is explicit in the Fathers (Basil’s Address to Young Men, Augustine’s On Christian Teaching), and the survival of Latin classics through monastic and Carolingian copying is documented manuscript by manuscript.
influences/rhetoric-and-education/popula: Either Christianity destroyed classical learning and plunged Europe into the Dark Ages, or the church alone heroically preserved it: both are common slogans.
influences/rhetoric-and-education/whatHi: Historians such as H.-I. Marrou, Werner Jaeger and Peter Brown show that ancient Christians had no separate school system: they went to the same grammarians and rhetors as pagans and took classical culture for granted, while arguing about its proper use. There were real losses and hostile acts — the destruction of the Serapeum in Alexandria (391), the killing of Hypatia (415), the reuse of classical manuscripts as palimpsests — and the decline of Roman institutions in the West shrank learning drastically. But most surviving Latin classics reached us through ninth-century Carolingian monastic copies, and Byzantium preserved Greek literature. The story is one of selective appropriation, not simple destruction or preservation.
influences/rhetoric-and-education/summar: Christian leaders were educated in classical rhetoric and literature, debated whether pagan books were safe, and in the end baptised the school curriculum. That decision shaped Christian preaching, exegesis and the medieval schools and universities.
influences/rhetoric-and-education/story:
Greek and Roman education followed a set path: reading and writing, then the grammarian who taught Homer or Virgil, then the rhetor who trained young men in public speaking on the model of Demosthenes and Cicero. This paideia was the badge of the elite throughout the Empire. Christians had no alternative schools; their children learned with pagans, and many converts — Justin, Cyprian, Lactantius, Augustine — were trained rhetors. Paul’s letters already use the forms of ancient rhetoric, and the Gospel had to be preached to audiences who expected eloquence.

The Fathers debated how far this culture could be trusted. Tertullian (On Idolatry 10) allowed Christians to learn literature but not to teach it, because teaching meant expounding the gods. Origen, according to his pupil Gregory Thaumaturgus, led students through logic, natural science, ethics and all the philosophers except atheists before Scripture. The crisis came in 362, when the Emperor Julian forbade Christians to teach the classics, arguing that they should not expound authors whose gods they rejected. Christians answered with fury: Gregory of Nazianzus protested in his invectives against Julian, and two Apollinarii rewrote Scripture in classical metres.

Gregory of Nazianzus and Basil of Caesarea had studied together in Athens c. 350–356, and Basil’s Address to Young Men on Greek Literature compared the Christian reader to a bee taking honey and leaving the poison. Jerome, an ardent Ciceronian, dreamt that Christ condemned him with the words ‘You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian’ (Letter 22.30, c. 384), yet he never ceased to write elegant Latin. Augustine, once professor of rhetoric at Milan, gave the decisive Latin answer in On Christian Teaching (396–426): pagan learning that is true can be taken over as the Israelites took the Egyptians’ gold (Exodus 12:35–36), and Book 4 adapts Cicero’s three styles of oratory for Christian preaching. John Chrysostom, pupil of the pagan rhetor Libanius, became the greatest preacher of the Greek church.

As Roman schools collapsed in the West, Christians took over the task of education. Boethius translated logic and wrote on music and arithmetic; Cassiodorus (c. 485–585) founded the monastery of Vivarium and wrote the Institutions to guide monks in sacred and secular learning; Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies (c. 630) summarised ancient knowledge; Bede taught grammar, computus and history at Jarrow. The seven liberal arts — grammar, rhetoric and dialectic (the trivium); arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy (the quadrivium) — became the basis of Carolingian, cathedral and finally university education. Most classical Latin texts survive because they were copied in Carolingian monasteries in the ninth century, though others perished or were scraped off for reuse, as Cicero’s On the Republic was, surviving beneath Augustine’s commentary on the Psalms.

The ambivalence never vanished. Gregory the Great rebuked Bishop Desiderius of Vienne in 601 for teaching grammar from pagan poets, though Gregory himself wrote polished Latin. Renaissance humanists such as Erasmus argued for a return to classical eloquence in theology, while Puritans and pietists periodically worried about pagan authors in Christian schools. Yet the decision of the Fathers to ‘spoil the Egyptians’ made the classical heritage part of Christian culture for the next millennium and a half.

influences/christ-sol-good-shepherd-art/: Christ as Sol, Orpheus and the Good Shepherd in early art
Graeco-Roman pastoral, Orphic and solar imagery: the ram-bearing shepherd (kriophoros), Orpheus taming the beasts, and Helios/Sol in his chariot
Christ depicted as the Good Shepherd, as a new Orpheus and as the radiant ‘Sun of righteousness’ in catacomb, sarcophagus and tomb art
Catacomb of Callixtus, Rome

The borrowing of visual types is well documented: the shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders, Orpheus with his lyre and Sol in a quadriga all existed in Roman art long before Christians used them, and Christian examples sit beside pagan ones in the same workshops and cemeteries. What was borrowed was a visual vocabulary, not a cult: the meanings Christians gave these images came from Psalm 23, John 10, Luke 15 and Malachi 4:2.
Early Christian art proves that Jesus was really a sun god or a rebranded pagan deity, because the earliest pictures of him are copied from Apollo, Orpheus and Sol Invictus.

Historians agree that pre-Constantinian Christian art took over existing Roman image types, as any new art in the Roman world had to; workshops produced sarcophagi with shepherds and seasons for pagan and Christian buyers alike. The ‘Good Shepherd’ is by far the commonest image of Christ before 313, and its biblical meaning is explicit in texts of the period. Orpheus images are rare and appear also in Jewish art (David as Orpheus in the Dura-Europos synagogue). The single famous ‘Christ-Helios’ mosaic, in the Mausoleum of the Julii beneath St Peter’s, is identified as Christ only because of the Jonah and fisherman scenes around it, and some scholars read it as Sol. Writers such as Clement of Alexandria consciously used Orpheus and the sun as metaphors for Christ, while Leo the Great complained of Christians who still bowed to the sun: the evidence shows adaptation of imagery and occasional popular confusion, not a solar origin for Christian belief.

The first Christian images of Christ borrowed the familiar Roman figures of the shepherd carrying a sheep, the singer Orpheus and the sun-god in his chariot, re-reading them through biblical texts about the Good Shepherd and the ‘Sun of righteousness’.

Christian art appears in the archaeological record only around AD 200, in the catacombs of Rome, on sarcophagi and in the house church at Dura-Europos on the Euphrates (decorated c. 232–256). It did not invent a new visual language. Its artists and patrons used the stock repertoire of Roman funerary art: banquets, orants (praying figures with raised hands), seasons, vines, fishermen and, above all, the youthful shepherd carrying a sheep across his shoulders. This kriophoros (‘ram-bearer’) type had a long pagan history, from archaic Greek votive statues to Calamis’s Hermes Kriophoros at Tanagra described by Pausanias, and in Roman art it had become a generic emblem of rural peace and philanthropy.

For Christians the figure carried precise biblical meaning: ‘I am the good shepherd’ (John 10:11), the shepherd who seeks the lost sheep (Luke 15:4–7), and the Lord who is ‘my shepherd’ in Psalm 23, a psalm associated with baptism and burial. Tertullian, c. 210–220, mentions the shepherd painted on Christian communion cups (De pudicitia 7 and 10), and the shepherd appears in the baptistery at Dura beside Adam and Eve. Robin Jensen counts the Good Shepherd as the most frequently depicted image of Christ before Constantine; only in the late fourth century, as Christ came to be shown enthroned and bearded, did the type fade.

Orpheus, the mythical singer whose music tamed wild beasts and who descended to the underworld, appears in a handful of Roman catacomb paintings (Domitilla, Callixtus, Peter and Marcellinus) and on some sarcophagi. Clement of Alexandria opens his Exhortation to the Greeks (c. 195) by contrasting Orpheus with Christ, the true singer of the ‘New Song’ who tames the wildest beasts, human beings. Jewish artists made the same move: the synagogue at Dura-Europos shows David playing the lyre in the pose of Orpheus. The image was a shared Mediterranean way of picturing harmony and the conquest of death, adopted by communities who gave it their own scriptural content.

Solar imagery is the most contested case. Malachi 4:2 promised the ‘sun of righteousness’ rising with healing in its wings, the Gospels describe Christ’s face shining ‘like the sun’ at the Transfiguration, and Christians prayed facing east. Clement calls Christ ‘the Sun of righteousness who drives his chariot over all’ (Protrepticus 11). In the Vatican necropolis, the mid-third-century Mausoleum M, the ‘Tomb of the Julii’, has a gold mosaic of a charioteer with rays behind his head, surrounded by Jonah, a fisherman and a shepherd; most scholars identify it as Christ-Helios, though Steven Hijmans and others caution that the figure is iconographically pure Sol. Pagan critics noticed the parallel: Tertullian reports that some thought the Christians worshipped the sun because they prayed eastwards and kept the ‘day of the sun’ (Apology 16; Ad nationes 1.13), a charge he rejects.

The church’s leaders were alert to the risk of confusion. Pope Leo the Great, preaching at Christmas c. 450 (Sermon 27), rebuked Christians who turned and bowed to the rising sun on the steps of St Peter’s before entering the basilica. The Council of Elvira (c. 306) had already ruled that pictures should not be painted on church walls, and a letter attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea discouraged images of Christ altogether. The verdict of modern scholarship, from André Grabar to Thomas Mathews and Jensen, is that early Christian art is a classic case of the borrowing of forms: Christians spoke the visual language of their culture while insisting, in their texts, on meanings drawn from Israel’s scriptures and the story of Jesus.
Christians bought sarcophagi and paid painters from the same Roman workshops as their pagan neighbours, choosing from an existing stock of motifs.
Ambiguous pastoral images (shepherds, vines, banquets) were selected because they could be read biblically without advertising a persecuted faith.
Apologists such as Clement of Alexandria and Justin presented Christ as the fulfilment of what was best in Greek myth and philosophy, encouraging visual parallels.
Biblical metaphors (shepherd, light, sun of righteousness) gave Christians a reason to adopt pagan types and fill them with new meaning.
From the later fourth century imperial and enthroned images of Christ displaced the youthful shepherd type.

Presented Christ as the true Orpheus and the ‘Sun of righteousness’ (Protrepticus 1 and 11), and in the Paedagogus (3.11) advised Christians which existing seal-ring motifs they could use.
Justin Martyr
Argued that the Word had sown ‘seeds’ of truth among the Greeks, a theology that made borrowing classical forms appear legitimate (2 Apology 13).
Eusebius of Caesarea
Freely used solar and imperial light imagery for Christ and the Logos in his orations, even while doubting the propriety of portraits of Christ.
Leo the Great
Rebuked Christians who bowed to the rising sun on the steps of St Peter’s before Christmas Mass, as a relic of pagan sun worship (Sermon 27.4).
